headline: High-risk shared-write orchestration pair: default shared state and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action hazards.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and both expose shared state mechanisms (Dify datastore; LangGraph checkpointer store). That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other's outputs from shared storage. No MCP or clipboard bridge is documented, so this is not high, but the shared workspace/state makes injection plausible in default deployments.
conditions: IF agent_a writes attacker-controlled text into shared datastore content that agent_b later parses as instructions
IF agent_b reads application-defined files or state from a shared workspace without provenance checks
mitigations: Add provenance tags to all shared state entries
Separate agent_a and agent_b workspaces
Treat shared file/state content as untrusted input
Require explicit allowlists for instruction-bearing fields
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance enforcement in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches knowledge base content and conversation logs, while agent_b touches application-defined graph state. Both have broad network egress and can read/write files, so sensitive data can flow between them through shared state or outputs in default setups. The profiles do not show a third-party upload that is uncontrollable, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF agent_a stores conversation logs or KB content in shared state accessible to agent_b
IF agent_b forwards graph state containing sensitive data to model providers or tools
mitigations: Restrict shared state to non-sensitive fields
Redact logs before cross-agent handoff
Use separate credentials for each agent
Disable file sharing between workspaces
requires-engineering: enforce data-class-based routing and redaction

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. Dify also runs server-side code tools in a sandbox container, while LangGraph is library-only with developer-wired tools; together they can still target the same host paths or mutable resources if deployed in one environment. That overlapping write surface makes destructive conflicts plausible by default.
conditions: IF both agents are deployed against the same writable directory or shared volume
IF developer-wired tools let agent_b modify resources that agent_a also writes
mitigations: Assign disjoint filesystem roots
Run each agent under separate OS users
Lock shared mutable resources before writes
Disable shell writes in one agent during coordination
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_b is a graph orchestrator that can treat upstream node outputs as inputs, and agent_a is an agent/workflow platform that can emit tool outputs and KB-derived text. If agent_b consumes agent_a's output without verification, errors or hallucinations can cascade into downstream actions. Because both can invoke tools and networked services, the blast radius can include real external actions.
conditions: IF agent_b routes agent_a output directly into action-taking nodes
IF agent_a-generated text is used as authoritative facts without validation
mitigations: Insert a verification step between agents
Require citations or structured schemas for handoff
Gate external actions behind human approval
Log and diff upstream outputs before execution
requires-engineering: add policy checks on downstream tool calls

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only open-source systems with broad network egress and storage of conversation logs or graph state. The profiles do not specify residency, retention, or certification boundaries, so a compliance mismatch is plausible but not proven. Because the same data classes can be persisted in both systems, differing retention or logging policies could create a medium compliance gap.
conditions: IF the deployment stores regulated data in agent_a conversation logs and agent_b graph state
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the two systems
mitigations: Classify regulated data before ingestion
Align retention settings across both systems
Document residency and processor roles
Purge logs on a fixed schedule
requires-engineering: implement unified compliance policy enforcement
